headline: Four ancient populations
body: Same species. Same biology. Measurably different bones.

headline: Modern height discussion
body: Receptors, signalling, supplements, drugs. A framework built entirely on what's happening inside one body.
punch: Anthropology asks a different question and gets a different answer.

headline: Researchers compared
body: Late Stone Age, Sadlermiut, Indian Knoll and Point Hope. Femur and humerus cortical thickness, and diaphyseal length, measured across populations.
punch: Skeletal growth compared at the level of whole populations.

headline: The differences
body: Not noise. Meaningful inter-population variation in how bone grew — in both how long bones got and how thick their walls became.
punch: Two different growth outcomes from the same human template.

headline: And the best explanation
body: Population-level differences in growth environment — nutrition, activity load, disease burden — accounted for the variation better than ancestry did.
punch: Environment wrote more of the outcome than inheritance.

headline: Which is a useful correction
body: Individual hormone optimisation is a very narrow lens. At population scale, the things that moved skeletal growth were load, food and illness.
punch: The biggest levers historically were the least glamorous ones.

headline: It also explains
body: Populations gained substantial height across generations without any genetic change — the same environmental levers, applied at scale, over decades.
punch: Genetics sets a range. Environment decides where in it you land.

headline: The limits
body: Skeletal remains can't tell you diet or activity directly — those are inferred. And population-level findings don't predict any individual outcome.
punch: Useful for perspective. Useless as a personal protocol.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
